title: The Opening, as if for the first time
hook: the Fatiha read with everything you now know (Surah 1)
tomorrow: one word in the Throne verse, two old readings. who's right?

segments.voice: Yesterday, calling by the names: Zakariya asked for an heir and called God the best of inheritors. The line: call him by name. The Names are gathered. Now we open the book itself, from its first page.
screen: `CALL HIM BY NAME.` → `NOW, THE BOOK ITSELF.`

segments.voice: You're telling a friend how great someone is, how kind, how fair, and then you turn around and that person is standing in the doorway. Mid-sentence, she becomes you. Every Muslim prayer has that moment in it. The Fatiha, the Opening, starts by talking about Allah: praise, Lord of the Worlds, the Beneficent, the Merciful, Owner of the Day of Judgment. Then, with no warning, it turns and speaks to Him. Why the switch?
screen: `SHE'S IN THE DOORWAY.` → `ABOUT HIM, THEN TO HIM.` → `WHY THE SWITCH?`

segments.voice: Here's the turn in Pickthall's words. First: "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds." Then, after the Day of Judgment: "Thee (alone) we worship; Thee (alone) we ask for help." He, then Thee. The solution is in a hadith qudsi, words the Prophet, peace be upon him, reported from Allah. Allah says He has divided the prayer between Himself and His servant, in two halves. When the servant says, praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds, Allah says: My servant has praised Me. At the Merciful: My servant has extolled Me. At the Day of Judgment: My servant has glorified Me. And at Thee alone we worship: this is between Me and My servant, and My servant shall have what he asks. So the switch is where the reply comes in. The Opening isn't a speech. It's a conversation, and each line gets an answer. That's the line to tell a friend tonight: in the hadith, the Fatiha is answered line by line, as it's said. And notice whose Lord He is in the very first line: not of one people, of the Worlds. These are the first words of the Qur'an, and the words said in every rak'ah of every prayer, to the last.
screen: `PRAISE BE TO ALLAH, LORD OF THE WORLDS.` · `HE, THEN THEE.` · `EACH LINE GETS AN ANSWER.` · `LORD OF THE WORLDS, NOT ONE PEOPLE.` · then, large: `FIRST WORDS, LAST WORDS.`

segments.voice: If you know the Fatiha, recite it once, as slowly as you can, and pause at the end of each line as if waiting for the reply. If you don't, say its first line in English, praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds, and leave the same pause after it.
The Opening: al-Fatiha, the first surah, a conversation with a reply after every line.
Carry it out the door: first words, last words, and a pause after each one. A new camp, open.

howItsDone: Muslims recite al-Fatiha in every rak'ah of every prayer, with Amin said after it; it is also recited at weddings, gatherings and for those who have died.

fork.setup: your little cousin, learning the Fatiha, asks: 'why does it say Lord of the Worlds? why not Lord of the Muslims?' what can you tell her?
options: the very first line names Him Lord of all the Worlds, not of one people.
it's a poetic plural; it really means Lord of the Muslims.
worlds means planets; that line is about outer space.
fork.reveal: "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds." the Qur'an's first words don't shrink Him to one group.

chat.says: dadi reads the fatiha SO slowly before fajr. pauses after every line. i speed-run it. does speed even matter
options: In the hadith, Allah answers every line. Dadi is leaving room for the reply.
Not really. Same words either way; as long as you finish, speed changes nothing.
Slow reciting is for scholars. Regular people are meant to keep it quick.
chat.meaning: Allah says He divided the prayer with His servant, and answers each line: 'My servant has praised Me.' The pause makes room.
